q: What are the notes of the guitar strings in standard tuning, from lowest to highest?
a: E-A-D-G-B-E (6th string to 1st string)

q: If you play the 5th fret of the 6th string (low E), what note are you playing?
a: A (same pitch as the open 5th string)

q: How many semitones does moving up one fret represent?
a: 1 semitone (half step)

q: What note is located at the 12th fret of any string?
a: The same note as the open string, one octave higher

q: In standard tuning, which two adjacent strings are NOT tuned a perfect 4th apart?
a: The G (3rd) and B (2nd) strings - they are a major 3rd apart (4 semitones instead of 5)

q: What is the MIDI note number range for a standard 6-string guitar in standard tuning?
a: E2 (MIDI note 40) to approximately E6 (MIDI note 88), depending on how many frets the guitar has

q: If you're in Drop D tuning, what note is the 6th string tuned to?
a: D (one whole step down from E)

q: What interval is created when you play the same fret on two adjacent strings (except G and B strings)?
a: Perfect 4th

q: In an open G tuning (D-G-D-G-B-D), what chord do you get when strumming all open strings?
a: G major chord

q: What are the five shapes in the CAGED system?
a: C, A, G, E, and D chord shapes that can be moved up and down the neck

q: How many positions/patterns are there for the minor pentatonic scale across the fretboard?
a: 5 positions (one for each note of the pentatonic scale)

q: In the A minor pentatonic scale (A-C-D-E-G), what is the "blue note" that creates the blues scale?
a: Eb (D#) - the flatted 5th

q: If you're playing position 1 of A minor pentatonic starting at the 5th fret, which frets will you primarily use?
a: Frets 5-8 (with most notes on frets 5 and 7)

q: What scale degree pattern defines the major scale?
a: W-W-H-W-W-W-H (Whole-Whole-Half-Whole-Whole-Whole-Half)

q: In the "3 notes per string" scale pattern, how many positions are needed to cover the major scale across the entire neck?
a: 7 positions (one starting on each scale degree)

q: What mode would you be playing if you use the C major scale pattern but resolve to D?
a: D Dorian mode

q: If you play only the white keys on piano (C-D-E-F-G-A-B-C) on guitar starting from the 8th fret of the 6th string, what key are you in?
a: C major (or A minor)

q: What is the formula for the harmonic minor scale?
a: W-H-W-W-H-W+H-H (or 2-1-2-2-1-3-1 in semitones)

q: Which scale has the pattern: whole step - whole step - whole step - whole step - whole step - whole step?
a: Whole tone scale

q: In E minor pentatonic (E-G-A-B-D), which notes from the full E natural minor scale are omitted?
a: F# and C (the 2nd and 6th scale degrees)

q: What three notes make up an E major power chord (E5) when played with root on the 6th string?
a: E (root), B (perfect 5th), E (octave)

q: In a barre chord using the E major shape moved to the 3rd fret, what chord are you playing?
a: G major

q: What notes comprise an open C major chord in standard voicing (X-3-2-0-1-0)?
a: C-E-G-C-E (from 5th string to 1st string, with 6th string muted)

q: Why do power chords work well with distortion?
a: They contain no 3rd, avoiding dissonant overtones; only root and 5th create clean, powerful sound

q: If you play strings 4-3-2 at frets 7-7-7, what chord are you playing?
a: A-D-F#, a D major triad in second inversion (A in the bass). String 4 at fret 7 is A, string 3 is D and string 2 is F#.

q: What is a "cowboy chord"?
a: An open position chord (typically C, A, G, E, D, Am, Em, Dm) played in first position

q: In the CAGED system, which shape would you use to play a C major chord with the root on the 5th string, 3rd fret?
a: A shape (moved to the 3rd fret)

q: What is the difference between Cmaj7 and C7 chords?
a: Cmaj7 has a major 7th (B), while C7 has a minor 7th (Bb)

q: If you play a sus4 chord and resolve it, which note moves and where does it go?
a: The 4th moves down by one semitone to the 3rd (e.g., in Csus4, F moves down to E)

q: What notes would you play for a shell voicing of Gmaj7 (just 3rd and 7th)?
a: B (major 3rd) and F# (major 7th)

q: When programming a downstroke strum in piano roll, in what order should the notes trigger?
a: Lowest to highest (bass strings first, treble strings last), with 3-5ms spacing

q: What velocity range is appropriate for the second note in a hammer-on?
a: 60-80 (lower than the picked note which would be 100-127)

q: How do you represent a whole-step bend in piano roll?
a: Start on one note, use pitch bend automation to raise it 2 semitones, or play the target note with pitch bend from below

q: What note length setting creates an authentic palm-muted sound in piano roll?
a: Very short/staccato (typically 1/16 note or shorter with gaps between notes)

q: When programming a pull-off from B to A, how should the velocities compare?
a: First note (B) should have higher velocity (picked), second note (A) should have lower velocity (pulled-off)

q: How far apart should notes be spaced when programming a realistic guitar strum?
a: 3-5 milliseconds between each string

q: For two-hand tapping, what is the typical velocity relationship between picked, tapped, and pulled-off notes?
a: Picked (100-127), tapped (90-110), pulled-off (70-90)

q: When creating a slide guitar part with portamento, should you use stepped pitches or continuous glide?
a: Continuous glide/portamento for smooth sliding between pitches

q: How do you create realistic artificial harmonics in piano roll?
a: Play notes 1-2 octaves higher than the fretted position, often at 12th fret (octave), 7th fret (octave+5th), or 5th fret (2 octaves)

q: What's the best way to humanize programmed guitar strums?
a: Slight timing variations, varied note spacing (3-5ms), subtle velocity differences, occasional ghost notes

q: Why are the keys of E, A, D, G, and C considered "guitar-friendly"?
a: They utilize open strings, allowing for easier fingering, fuller resonance, and characteristic guitar tone

q: What is the musical interval between the 5th fret of the 6th string and the 7th fret of the 5th string?
a: Perfect 5th (A to E)

q: If you're playing in E minor and want to add a modal interchange chord from E major, what chord could you borrow?
a: A major (IV from E major) or C# minor (vi from E major), among others

q: In a I-IV-V progression in the key of A, what chords would you play?
a: A major - D major - E major

q: What is the relationship between the A minor pentatonic scale and the C major pentatonic scale?
a: They contain the same notes (they are relative scales - Am is the relative minor of C major)

q: If you're playing a 12-bar blues in E, what are the three main chords?
a: E7 (I), A7 (IV), and B7 (V)

q: What interval creates the distinctive sound of a major chord versus a minor chord?
a: The 3rd - major 3rd (4 semitones) sounds happy, minor 3rd (3 semitones) sounds sad

q: In Drop D tuning, what advantage does the low D provide for playing power chords?
a: You can play power chords on the bottom 3 strings with just one finger barred across one fret

q: If you're playing in the Dorian mode starting on A (A Dorian), what major scale shares the same notes?
a: G major (A Dorian is the 2nd mode of G major)

q: When programming a guitar solo in A minor, which notes from the A blues scale create the most tension and typically resolve downward?
a: The blue note (Eb/D#) creates tension and typically resolves down to D; the G can also create tension resolving down to F or E

q: What is a pinch harmonic and how would you represent it in piano roll?
a: A pinch harmonic is created by lightly touching the string with the thumb while picking, producing a high-pitched squeal. In piano roll, use very high notes (2-3 octaves above fretted position) with short duration and pitch bend vibrato.

q: Explain the difference between natural vibrato and mechanical vibrato on guitar.
a: Natural vibrato = slight pitch variations created by finger movement (±1/4 to 1/2 semitone). Mechanical vibrato = tremolo/whammy bar creates wider pitch variations. Program with pitch bend automation: subtle (±50 cents) for natural, wider for whammy bar.

q: What is sweep picking and how does it affect note timing in piano roll?
a: Sweep picking is one continuous pick motion across several strings. The notes are tightly spaced but still separate: about 15-60 ms apart (for example 16th or 32nd notes at a fast tempo), not 1-3 ms, which would sound like a block chord. Keep velocity even (90-110) for a fluid arpeggiated sound.

q: How do you program a realistic guitar pick scrape in piano roll?
a: Create a descending chromatic or atonal run with very short note durations, low velocity (30-50), and rapid timing. Often starts high and descends to low strings, with increasing velocity at the end.

q: What is economy picking and how does it differ from alternate picking?
a: Economy picking = pick moves in same direction when crossing strings (more efficient). Alternate picking = strict down-up-down-up pattern. In piano roll, economy picking might have slight timing variations on string crosses, while alternate is more metronomic.

q: How would you program a chicken picking (hybrid picking) pattern in piano roll?
a: Combination of picked notes (higher velocity 100-120) and plucked notes (medium velocity 80-100). Country/funk style uses syncopated rhythms with sharp staccato notes and occasional ghost notes (velocity 40-60).

q: What is a pre-bend and how do you create it in piano roll?
a: Bend the string before picking so the note starts at target pitch. In piano roll: use pitch bend automation set to +2 semitones (or desired interval) before note trigger, then optionally release during or after the note.

q: Explain the "rake" technique and its velocity characteristics.
a: Rake = quick muted notes leading to a target note, creating percussive attack. Program as 2-4 very short muted notes (velocity 20-40, very short duration) immediately before the main note (velocity 100-127).

q: What is tapping harmonics and what MIDI note range represents it?
a: Tapping at harmonic nodes (12th, 7th, 5th fret positions) produces bell-like tones. Use MIDI notes 2-3 octaves above normal fretted position, often with modulation and delay effects. Very short attack with some sustain.

q: How do you differentiate between a dive bomb and a scoop in pitch bend programming?
a: Dive bomb = pitch bend downward from played note (start at 0, bend down to -12 or more semitones). Scoop = start below target pitch and bend up into it (start at -2 to -5 semitones, bend to 0).

q: What makes the Phrygian mode sound "Spanish" or "exotic"?
a: The flatted 2nd scale degree (b2) creates a distinctive half-step between root and 2nd, characteristic of flamenco and Spanish music. In E Phrygian: E-F-G-A-B-C-D.

q: How would you use the Lydian mode over a IV chord to create a "dreamy" sound?
a: The #4 (or #11) in Lydian creates floating, ethereal quality. Over F major in key of C, use F Lydian (F-G-A-B-C-D-E) emphasizing the B natural for the characteristic sound.

q: What is the Mixolydian mode and over which chord type is it commonly used?
a: Major scale with b7. Formula: W-W-H-W-W-H-W. Used over dominant 7th chords (e.g., G Mixolydian over G7). Creates bluesy, rock sound. The b7 provides dominant function.

q: What scale would you use to solo over a half-diminished chord (m7b5)?
a: Locrian mode (7th mode of major scale). For Bm7b5, use B Locrian (B-C-D-E-F-G-A) which has b2, b3, b5, and b7 - matching the chord tones.

q: Explain the difference between melodic minor ascending and the Dorian mode.
a: Melodic minor has raised 6th and 7th vs natural minor. Dorian has raised 6th only. A melodic minor ascending: A-B-C-D-E-F#-G#. A Dorian: A-B-C-D-E-F#-G.

q: What is the Phrygian dominant scale and in what genres is it commonly used?
a: 5th mode of harmonic minor. Has b2, major 3rd, and b6. Formula: H-W+H-H-W-H-W. Creates Middle Eastern, metal, and flamenco sounds. E Phrygian dominant: E-F-G#-A-B-C-D.

q: How do you form a diminished scale and what is its symmetrical property?
a: Alternating half and whole steps. Two types: half-whole (H-W-H-W...) and whole-half (W-H-W-H...). Symmetrical = repeats every minor 3rd (3 frets), so only 3 unique diminished scales exist.

q: What is the altered scale (Super Locrian) and when would you use it?
a: 7th mode of melodic minor. Contains all altered tones: b9, #9, #11, b13. Used over altered dominant chords (7alt, 7#5, 7b9). Creates maximum tension before resolution.

q: What makes the harmonic major scale unique?
a: Major scale with b6. Creates exotic sound similar to harmonic minor but from major scale. C harmonic major: C-D-E-F-G-Ab-B. The W+H interval (G-Ab-B) creates distinctive sound.

q: Which scale shares all the same notes as C major but starts on A?
a: A natural minor (Aeolian mode). This is the relative minor relationship - all white keys. A-B-C-D-E-F-G.

q: What notes comprise a Cmaj9 chord and how would you voice it on guitar?
a: C-E-G-B-D (root, 3rd, 5th, 7th, 9th). Guitar voicings often omit the 5th: C-E-B-D, or the rootless E-B-D-G, which is also Em7 and works over a C bass note.

q: What is a slash chord and how is C/E different from C major?
a: Slash chord = chord with specific bass note. C/E means C major chord with E in bass (first inversion). Written as E-G-C from low to high instead of C-E-G.

q: How do you construct an add9 chord and how does it differ from a 9th chord?
a: Add9 = triad + 9th, no 7th. Cadd9: C-E-G-D. A 9th chord (Cmaj9 or C9) includes the 7th. Add9 has brighter, more open sound without 7th.

q: What is a 6/9 chord and in what style is it commonly used?
a: Major triad + 6th + 9th, no 7th. C6/9: C-E-G-A-D. Jazz, bossa nova, and pop use it for sophisticated, non-dominant endings. Sweet, stable sound.

q: Explain the function of a secondary dominant chord.
a: Dominant chord that resolves to a chord other than tonic. In C major, D7 (V7/V) resolves to G (V). Creates temporary key change feeling, adds harmonic interest.

q: What is a tritone substitution and how does it work?
a: Replace V7 with bII7 (dominant chord a tritone away). In C major, replace G7 with Db7, both resolve to Cmaj. They share the same 3rd and 7th (enharmonically).

q: How do you voice a drop 2 chord voicing on guitar?
a: Take a close-position chord and drop the second note from the top down an octave. Cmaj7 close: C-E-G-B. The second note from the top is G, so drop 2 is G-C-E-B (low to high). The wider spacing is common in jazz.

q: What is a quartal voicing and how does it differ from tertian harmony?
a: Built in 4ths instead of 3rds. C quartal: C-F-Bb-Eb (stacked 4ths). Sounds open, modern, ambiguous. Jazz and fusion use extensively. Tertian = traditional 3rd-based triads/7ths.

q: What makes a dominant 13th chord different from other 13th chords?
a: Dominant 13th (G13) has minor 7th, making it dominant function. Contains: G-B-D-F-A-C-E (R-3-5-b7-9-11-13). Major 13th (Gmaj13) has major 7th. Typically omit 11th.

q: How do you create a sus2 to major resolution on guitar?
a: Replace 3rd with 2nd, then resolve to major 3rd. Csus2 (C-D-G) → C major (C-E-G). The D resolves up to E. Creates tension and release, common in rock/pop.

q: What is a gallop rhythm and how do you program it in guitar parts?
a: Metal rhythm of one longer note followed by two quick ones. Pattern: 8th-16th-16th (the reverse, 16th-16th-8th, is also used). Program with power chords, palm muting and tight timing. Example: E-E-E (long-short-short).

q: How do you create a reggae guitar skank rhythm in piano roll?
a: Staccato chords on the off-beats (the "and" of each beat). Mute strings heavily (very short notes, 1/16 or shorter) at medium velocity (60-80). The drums, not the guitar, emphasise beats 2 and 4 (the one-drop).

q: What is a polymetric pattern and give an example for guitar?
a: Two different meters played simultaneously. Example: 3/4 pattern over 4/4 time signature. Creates interesting rhythmic tension. Tool and King Crimson use extensively.

q: Explain the difference between swing at 66% and straight 16th notes.
a: Straight 16ths = evenly spaced. Swing (66% or 2:1 ratio) = first of each pair is twice as long. At 66%, first note gets 2/3 of beat, second gets 1/3. Creates triplet feel.

q: What is a hemiola and how would you create it on guitar?
a: A rhythmic pattern in which two beats of three are felt against three of two: in 6/8, accenting every second eighth note (3 accents per bar) creates a 3/4 feel against the usual 3+3 grouping. Common in Spanish and Latin music.

q: How do you program a realistic funk guitar rhythm with ghost notes?
a: Syncopated 16th note pattern with accents on off-beats. Ghost notes (velocity 20-40) between accented notes (velocity 90-120). Tight, percussive, palm-muted sound. Staccato.

q: What is a displaced accent and how does it create groove?
a: Accent on unexpected beat. Instead of accenting 1 and 3, accent "&" of 2 or other off-beats. Creates syncopation and forward motion. Common in funk and jazz.

q: How do you create a latin clave-based guitar rhythm?
a: Follow the 3-2 or 2-3 clave pattern. 3-2 son clave in one bar of 4/4 hits on beat 1, the "a" of 1 (1.75), the "and" of 2 (2.5), the "and" of 3 (3.5) and beat 4. Program guitar chords or bass notes on the clave hits, with slight anticipation for an authentic feel.

q: What is the shuffle feel and what's the mathematical ratio?
a: Triplet-based feel where 8th notes are played as first and third note of triplet. Ratio is 2:1 (first note twice as long). Different from straight 16ths. Blues, jazz standard.

q: How do you program a realistic palm-muted breakdown rhythm for metal?
a: Tight 16th or 32nd notes on low strings with very short duration (staccato), medium-low velocity (70-90), following kick drum pattern. Often uses syncopation and rests for impact.

q: What chord progression defines the 12-bar blues and what are the chords in E?
a: I-I-I-I-IV-IV-I-I-V-IV-I-V (or I). In E: E7-E7-E7-E7-A7-A7-E7-E7-B7-A7-E7-B7. Each numeral represents one bar.

q: What makes a jazz ii-V-I progression sound more sophisticated than I-IV-V?
a: Uses diatonic chord function with 7th chords and creates stronger voice leading. In C: Dm7-G7-Cmaj7. The tritone in G7 (B-F) resolves inward and outward: B up to C (the root) and F down to E (the 3rd of Cmaj7).

q: How would you voice a Hendrix-style dominant 7#9 chord?
a: E7#9 (Hendrix chord): E-G#-D-G (low to high). Contains both major 3rd (G#) and minor 3rd (enharmonic to #9). Creates bluesy, funky dissonance. Play with distortion.

q: What scale and approach notes work best over a flamenco progression in E Phrygian?
a: E Phrygian (E-F-G-A-B-C-D) or E Phrygian dominant (E-F-G#-A-B-C-D). Emphasize b2 (F) and major 3rd (G#). Use rapid chromatic runs and ornaments.

q: In country guitar, what are the characteristics of a chicken-picked lick?
a: Hybrid picking (pick + fingers), fast 16th note patterns, string skipping, open string drones. Bright, percussive sound. Often in Mixolydian or major pentatonic with chromatic approaches.

q: How do you program a realistic metal gallop with triplet variation?
a: Combination of 16th note gallops and 16th note triplets. Palm-muted low string power chords, tight timing. Velocities 95-120. Example: 16th-16th-8th followed by triplet on next beat.

q: What defines a bossa nova guitar comp pattern?
a: Syncopated pattern in 2/4 or 4/4 with emphasis on off-beats. Soft fingerstyle or light pick. Jazz voicings (maj7, m7, 6/9). Pattern: bass note on 1, chord on 2&, bass on 3, chord on 4.

q: In blues-rock, how do you create the "Eric Clapton" tone programmatically?
a: Combination of technique and effects: string bends with vibrato, minor pentatonic + blues scale, medium velocity (75-95), slight pitch bend vibrato at phrase ends, use of the b5 (blue note).

q: What makes a surf rock guitar rhythm distinctive?
a: Fast tremolo picking on single notes or dyads, reverb-heavy sound, staccato notes, often in minor keys. Rapid 16th or 32nd notes with consistent velocity (90-100). Think Dick Dale.

q: How would you program a progressive rock odd-meter riff like Tool or Dream Theater?
a: Use time signatures like 7/8, 11/8, or 13/16. Palm-muted power chords with polymetric patterns. Accent pattern creates groove (e.g., 7/8 as 3+2+2). Tight timing, medium-high velocity (90-110).

q: How many keys does a standard piano have?
a: 88 keys (52 white keys and 36 black keys)

q: What is the name of the white key immediately to the left of any group of two black keys?
a: C (the "landmark" note for finding your position on the keyboard)

q: What is Middle C in scientific pitch notation, and what is its MIDI note number?
a: C4 in scientific pitch notation, MIDI note 60

q: What pattern of black keys helps you locate the note F on the piano?
a: F is immediately to the left of the group of three black keys

q: How many octaves does a standard 88-key piano span?
a: Just over 7 octaves (A0 to C8)

q: What is the interval between any white key and the black key immediately to its right?
a: One semitone (half step) - the black key is the sharp of the white key

q: Which two pairs of white keys have no black key between them?
a: E-F and B-C (these are natural semitones)

q: What is the typical playing range for most pop and rock piano parts?
a: C3 to C6 (three octaves centered around middle C)

q: If you play C and E together, how many semitones apart are they?
a: 4 semitones (a major 3rd)

q: What are the white keys on a piano named in order?
a: C-D-E-F-G-A-B, then the pattern repeats

q: What is the fingering pattern for a C major scale in the right hand?
a: 1-2-3-1-2-3-4-5 (thumb crosses under after finger 3)

q: How many sharps or flats are in the key of C major?
a: Zero - C major has no sharps or flats (all white keys)

q: What is the relative minor of C major?
a: A minor (shares the same key signature, starts on the 6th degree)

q: In the key of G major, which note is sharped?
a: F# (the 7th degree of the scale)

q: What scale uses only the black keys on the piano?
a: F# major pentatonic (or Gb major pentatonic) - also the enharmonic Db major pentatonic

q: What is the formula for the harmonic minor scale in whole and half steps?
a: W-H-W-W-H-W+H-H (whole-half-whole-whole-half-whole&half-half)

q: If you start on D and play only white keys, what mode are you playing?
a: D Dorian (the 2nd mode of C major)

q: What interval is created by playing C and G together?
a: Perfect 5th (7 semitones)

q: How many notes are in a pentatonic scale?
a: 5 notes (penta = five)

q: In a chromatic scale starting on C, what is the 7th note?
a: F# or Gb (C-C#-D-D#-E-F-F#...)

q: What three notes make up a C major triad in root position?
a: C-E-G (root, major 3rd, perfect 5th)

q: What is the difference between a C major chord and a C minor chord?
a: The 3rd - C major has E (major 3rd), C minor has Eb (minor 3rd)

q: What four notes comprise a Cmaj7 chord?
a: C-E-G-B (root, major 3rd, perfect 5th, major 7th)

q: What is a "shell voicing" for a C7 chord?
a: Playing just the essential tones: C (root), E (3rd), and Bb (7th), often omitting the 5th

q: If you play C-F-G, what type of chord is this?
a: Csus4 (suspended 4th chord - replaces the 3rd with the 4th)

q: In a first inversion C major chord, which note is in the bass?
a: E (the 3rd becomes the lowest note: E-G-C)

q: What is a "10th" interval, and why is it important in piano voicing?
a: An octave plus a 3rd: 16 semitones for a major 10th (15 for a minor 10th). Important because a 10th in the left hand creates a fuller sound than a plain 3rd in the bass register, and it is easier to reach than it looks.

q: What notes would you play for a rootless Cmaj9 voicing (common in jazz)?
a: E-G-B-D (3rd, 5th, 7th, 9th - omitting the root C)

q: What is the difference between a rolled chord and a blocked chord?
a: Rolled = notes played in quick succession (arpeggiated); Blocked = all notes played simultaneously

q: In stride piano, what does the left hand typically play on beats 1 and 3?
a: Bass notes (root or root and 5th of the chord)

q: When programming an Alberti bass pattern in C major, what is the note order?
a: C-G-E-G (root-5th-3rd-5th, repeated)

q: What MIDI CC number controls the sustain pedal?
a: CC64 (values 0-63 = off, 64-127 = on)

q: What velocity range represents piano (soft) playing?
a: Approximately 40-60 (pp to p dynamic range)

q: How should you program a realistic glissando in piano roll?
a: Rapid succession of notes (white or black keys) with slight timing offset (2-5ms apart) and increasing velocity

q: For a Chopin-style waltz accompaniment in 3/4 time, what is the left hand pattern?
a: Bass note on beat 1, chord on beats 2 and 3

q: When programming a piano tremolo, what note duration should you use?
a: Very short notes (1/32 or 1/64) repeated rapidly, with slight velocity variation

q: How do you create a realistic rolled chord ascending in piano roll?
a: Offset each note by 5-15ms, starting with lowest note, ending with highest

q: What velocity value typically represents fortissimo (very loud) playing?
a: 100-127 (ff to fff dynamic range)

q: For authentic two-hand independence, what should you avoid in piano roll programming?
a: Impossible stretches (more than an octave per hand), overlapping hands in impossible ways, or patterns that require more than 10 fingers

q: How should sustain pedal be used when changing chords to avoid muddiness?
a: Release pedal briefly during chord changes (syncopated pedaling), then re-engage after new chord starts

q: In a ii-V-I progression in C major, what are the three chords?
a: Dm7 (ii) - G7 (V) - Cmaj7 (I)

q: What is the purpose of using a Vsus4 to V resolution?
a: Creates tension and release; the 4th resolves down to the 3rd, strengthening the pull to the I chord

q: In stride piano, what interval is typically played on beat 2 of the left hand?
a: Usually a mid-range chord. The 10ths belong on the bass beats (1 and 3); beat 2 and 4 take the chord.

q: What is the I-V-vi-IV progression in the key of F major?
a: F - C - Dm - Bb

q: Why should you avoid playing small intervals (2nds, 3rds) in the bass register (below C3)?
a: They create muddy, unclear sound due to low frequency overtones clashing

q: What is "comping" in jazz piano?
a: Rhythmic, syncopated chord accompaniment that supports a soloist, typically using shell voicings on off-beats

q: In gospel piano, where do runs typically occur in relation to the beat?
a: Leading into the downbeat (usually on beat 4, resolving to beat 1)

q: What is the characteristic of a Lydian mode that makes it sound "dreamy"?
a: The raised 4th (#4 or #11), which creates an augmented 4th from the root

q: When using parallel motion (planing), why does it work despite breaking traditional voice leading rules?
a: Creates impressionistic, colorful sound; uniform motion prevents individual voices from standing out, creating a cohesive harmonic wash

q: In a montuno pattern (Latin piano), which hand typically plays the repetitive syncopated figure?
a: Right hand (while left hand plays bass tumbao pattern)

q: What is the difference between sostenuto pedal (CC66) and sustain pedal (CC64)?
a: Sostenuto sustains only notes already being held when pedal is pressed; sustain pedal sustains all notes played while pedal is down

q: In a diminished 7th chord, what is the interval between each consecutive note?
a: Minor 3rd (3 semitones) - creates a symmetrical chord structure

q: What makes a "Neapolitan sixth" chord unique in classical harmony?
a: It's a major chord built on the lowered 2nd scale degree, typically used in first inversion

q: How do you voice a quartal chord, and what genre commonly uses it?
a: Stack notes in 4ths (e.g., C-F-Bb-Eb); common in jazz and modern classical music

q: What is the relationship between C Lydian and G major scale?
a: They share the same notes - C Lydian is the 4th mode of G major

q: What is a drop 3 voicing and how does it differ from drop 2?
a: Drop 3 = take a close-position chord and drop the third note from the top down an octave. Cmaj7 close: C-E-G-B. The third note from the top is E, so drop 3 is E-C-G-B (low to high). Wider spread than drop 2 (G-C-E-B), often used in solo piano.

q: How do you voice a So What chord (Dm11) like Bill Evans?
a: A quartal voicing with a major 3rd on top, as played by Bill Evans: E-A-D-G-B (low to high), three perfect 4ths and a major 3rd. It omits the 3rd of Dm11 and sounds open and modern. Use both hands: the left plays the lower notes, the right the upper ones.

q: What is a cluster chord and in what context would you use it?
a: Adjacent notes played together (e.g., C-D-E or C-Db-D). Creates dissonance/tension. Used in modern classical, jazz, and cinematic music for dramatic effect or texture.

q: How do you voice a rootless A section voicing for a ii-V-I in C?
a: Dm7: F-A-C-E (3-5-7-9). G7: F-A-B-E (7-9-3-13). Cmaj7: E-G-B-D (3-5-7-9). Only one note moves by half-step between each chord (C to B, then F to E, A to G and E to D to land on Cmaj7). Left hand plays roots, right hand plays the guide tones and extensions without roots.

q: What is the difference between close and open position voicing?
a: Close position = all notes within an octave (C-E-G-B in one octave). Open position = notes spread beyond an octave (C3-G3-E4-B4). Open position sounds fuller, less muddy.

q: How would you voice a Kenny Barron-style Maj7#11 chord?
a: Use both hands: Left hand - root and 7th (C-B). Right hand - 3rd, #11, 9th (E-F#-D). Creates lush, sophisticated sound. The #11 adds Lydian color.

q: What is a spread voicing and how do you create one?
a: Voicing with intervals larger than an octave between some voices. Example: C3-G3-E4-B4-D5 for Cmaj9. Creates spacious, orchestral sound. Common in solo piano and ballads.

q: Explain the upper structure triad concept in jazz piano.
a: Play a triad in the right hand over the left hand's root and 7th. For G13#11: left hand G and F, right hand an A major triad (A-C#-E = 9, #11 and 13). Creates colorful extensions with one simple shape.

q: How do you voice a diminished 7th chord to create maximum tension?
a: Use all four notes close together (e.g., C-Eb-Gb-A) for compact tension. Or spread across hands for dramatic effect. Symmetrical = can resolve to multiple keys.

q: What is the McCoy Tyner quartal voicing style?
a: Stacked perfect 4ths in left hand, melodic line in right. Example: left hand plays D-G-C-F, right hand improvises. Creates powerful, modal jazz sound. Omits 3rds.

q: What is the bebop scale and how does it create smooth lines over changes?
a: Major or dominant scale with added chromatic passing tone. C bebop major: C-D-E-F-G-G#-A-B. The 8-note scale aligns chord tones on downbeats when playing 8th notes.

q: How do you practice two-octave scales with proper fingering for both hands?
a: Right hand usually 1-2-3-1-2-3-4-5 (thumb crosses under 3). Left hand often 5-4-3-2-1-3-2-1 (crosses over). Practice hands separately first, then together.

q: What modal interchange options exist when playing in C major?
a: Borrow from C minor, C Dorian, C Mixolydian, etc. Common borrowed chords: Fm, Ab, Bb, Eb from C minor. Creates emotional depth while staying in "C."

q: In what order should you practice the modes for maximum understanding?
a: Start with most common: Ionian (major), Aeolian (minor), then Dorian, Mixolydian, Phrygian, Lydian, finally Locrian. Focus on characteristic note of each mode.

q: How do you use the melodic minor scale in jazz improvisation?
a: Use the same scale ascending and descending (unlike classical). Gives access to altered dominant sounds: the altered scale is the melodic minor a half step above the dominant's root, so F melodic minor over E7alt provides all the alterations (b9, #9, #11, b13).

q: What is the symmetrical augmented scale and over what chord is it used?
a: The augmented scale alternates a minor 3rd and a half step (or the reverse): C-D#-E-G-G#-B. It is symmetrical, repeating every major 3rd, so there are only 4 distinct augmented scales. Used over augmented triads and maj7#5 chords.

q: How do you approach chord-scale relationships in modern jazz?
a: Match scale to chord quality: Major 7 = Ionian or Lydian, m7 = Dorian or Aeolian, 7 = Mixolydian or altered, m7b5 = Locrian. Consider harmonic context.

q: What is the blues scale and how does it differ from minor pentatonic?
a: Minor pentatonic + b5 (blue note). C blues: C-Eb-F-Gb-G-Bb. The Gb creates characteristic blues tension and can be approached/resolved chromatically.

q: How do you create a convincing gospel piano run connecting I to IV?
a: Use chromatic approach notes and scale tones. C to F: C-D-Eb-E-F or C-Db-D-E-F. Start slow, accelerate into the IV chord. End on chord tone. Increase velocity.

q: What is the Lydian Chromatic Concept and how does it apply to piano?
a: George Russell's theory: Lydian is the "unity" of a chord. Any chord can be approached through its Lydian mode. Creates outside/inside harmonic possibilities.

q: How do you program an authentic New Orleans second-line piano rhythm?
a: Syncopated 16th notes with bass line walking on 1-3, chords on off-beats. Left hand: root-5th pattern with syncopation. Right hand: punctuated chords and runs. Swing feel.

q: What defines a classical Baroque-style left hand pattern (Alberti bass)?
a: Broken chord pattern: lowest-highest-middle-highest. In C: C-G-E-G repeated. Provides harmonic rhythm and motion. Mozart and Haydn used extensively. Keeps steady pulse.

q: How do you create an authentic boogie-woogie bass line?
a: 8-to-the-bar pattern using walking bass with triplets or straight 8ths. Common pattern: root-3rd-5th-6th or root-3rd-5th-b7. Stays in lower register (C2-C3). Driving rhythm.

q: What is the clave son pattern and how does it apply to piano montuno?
a: 3-2 son clave on a 16-step grid: X..X..X...X.X... (hits on steps 1, 4, 7, 11 and 13; the 2-3 version starts on the two-side). The montuno follows this rhythm: the right hand plays a syncopated chord pattern and the left hand plays the tumbao bass, aligned with the clave.

q: How do you program realistic rubato in a romantic piano piece?
a: Gradual tempo changes before important notes/chords. Slight ritardando at phrase endings, accelerando building tension. Use tempo automation or manual note placement off grid.

q: What characterizes a Fats Waller stride piano left hand pattern?
a: Strong bass notes on 1 & 3 (often using 10ths), mid-range chords on 2 & 4. Left hand "strides" across keyboard. Bouncy, rhythmic feel. Right hand improvises/states melody.

q: How do you create an authentic ragtime syncopation?
a: Right hand plays syncopated melody (notes on off-beats, especially before beat 1). Left hand maintains steady boom-chick (bass-chord) pattern. Creates "ragged time" feel.

q: What is the característ ica left hand pattern in Brazilian bossa nova piano?
a: The characteristic left hand pattern in Brazilian bossa nova piano: a syncopated bass line emphasizing beats 1, 2&, 3 and 4&. Often the root on 1, the 5th on 2&, the root on 3 and a chromatic approach on 4&. It creates a samba-influenced groove.

q: How do you program a convincing church/gospel two-hand rhythmic pattern?
a: Both hands play chords rhythmically together with syncopation. Heavy use of sus4 resolutions, major-minor voice movement. Emphasis on 2 & 4. Often uses triplet feels and fills.

q: What defines a classical waltz accompaniment pattern beyond just 3/4 time?
a: Bass note on beat 1 (root or root+5th), chord on beats 2-3. Often oom-pah-pah feel. Right hand may add melody or countermelody. Chopin adds harmonic sophistication.

q: How do you program a realistic piano glissando with dynamics?
a: Rapid succession of notes (white or black keys only), starting slow and accelerating. Velocity starts medium (60-70), increases to high (100-120). Spacing: start 10ms apart, end 2ms apart.

q: What is the difference between a trill and a tremolo in classical piano?
a: Trill = rapid alternation between two adjacent notes (e.g., C-D-C-D). Tremolo = rapid repetition of single note OR alternation between two notes of any interval. Both create sustained effect.

q: How do you create a convincing grace note (acciaccatura) in MIDI?
a: Very short note (1/64 or shorter) just before main note (1-10ms before), low velocity (40-60), usually one semitone above or below target. Quickly resolves to main note.

q: What is a Viennese trill and how does it differ from a regular trill?
a: Starts on the upper auxiliary note, then alternates with the main note. A regular trill (in the modern convention) starts on the main note. Upper-note start: D-C-D-C-D-C versus main-note start: C-D-C-D-C-D. The term "Viennese trill" is not standard, but starting on the upper note was normal Baroque and Classical practice.

q: How do you program sympathetic resonance using MIDI CC?
a: Use sostenuto pedal (CC66) to hold bass notes while playing melody staccato above. Or extend certain note lengths while sustain pedal is modulated. Creates harp-like shimmer effect.

q: What is the una corda pedal effect and how is it different from just reducing velocity?
a: Una corda (soft pedal, CC67) shifts hammers to strike fewer strings, changing timbre to softer, mellower tone. Velocity reduction only changes volume, not timbral quality.

q: How do you create a piano cluster glissando like in contemporary classical music?
a: Multiple adjacent notes (forearm cluster) sliding chromatically up or down. Program as chromatic runs with 3-5 simultaneous notes moving in parallel. High velocity, chaotic feel.

q: What is inside-the-piano extended technique and how could you represent it?
a: Plucking strings, hitting strings with mallets, etc. In MIDI: use unusual velocity ranges, very short/long notes, pitch bends, and combine with non-piano sounds. Experimental timbres.

q: How do you program a realistic piano string dampening effect?
a: Very short note durations (staccato) with release time at 0. Velocity 40-70 for muted effect. Or automation of sustain pedal to create choked notes. Percussive, muted timbre.

q: What is half-pedaling and how do you represent it in MIDI?
a: Sustain pedal partially depressed (CC64 value 40-60 instead of 0-127). Creates subtle sustain without full resonance. Allows harmonic clarity while maintaining some connection between notes.

q: What is a Neapolitan sixth chord and how would you voice it on piano?
a: bII major chord in first inversion. In C major: Db major chord (Db-F-Ab) with F in bass. Voicing: F2-Db3-F3-Ab3. Resolves powerfully to V or I. Classical dramatic device.

q: How do you voice and resolve an Italian augmented sixth chord?
a: In C major: Ab-C-F# (bVI, I, #IV). Resolves outward to G (V). Left hand: Ab2, right hand: C-F#. Both voices move outward by half-step to G. Creates powerful dominant preparation.

q: What is a French augmented sixth chord and how does it function?
a: bVI-I-II-#IV. In C: Ab-C-D-F#. Creates dominant preparation. Resolves to V (G). More dissonant than Italian aug 6th due to added D (major 2nd).

q: How do you use parallel dominant 13th chords (planing) for modern jazz sound?
a: Move entire 13th chord shape chromatically. C13 shape (C-E-G-Bb-D-A) moved up to Db13, D13, etc. Breaks voice leading rules but creates lush, cinematic harmony.

q: What is the difference between functional and non-functional harmony in piano performance?
a: Functional = chords have directional pull (V→I, ii→V). Non-functional = chords chosen for color/texture (modal, planing). Functional uses voice leading; non-functional uses parallel motion or stepwise bass.
